name: Cheek lift

lead: A cheek lift, or midface lift, moves sagging cheek tissue and the malar fat pad upward for a fuller, more youthful midface. Some younger men who feel their cheeks look flat or hollow discuss it for a more defined look.

Surgeons lift the cheek soft tissue, sometimes beneath the periosteum, through incisions at the lower eyelid, hairline or inside the mouth, and fix it higher. Published results come mostly from surgeon-authored technique series on ageing faces, often combined with eyelid surgery or a facelift; use in young men has not been studied.

paras: It is done by a surgeon, often as part of a wider facial rejuvenation plan. Milder cases are sometimes approached with non-surgical options such as threads, fillers or energy-based devices. Recovery involves swelling and bruising over weeks.

Listed complications include haematoma, nerve injury, scarring and eyelid malposition; smoking raises the risk of skin necrosis. Results are documented mainly in surgeon-authored series rather than controlled trials.

angle.text: People want a fuller, higher midface instead of flat or sagging cheeks. Surgeons reposition the cheek soft tissue and malar fat pad upward and fix it there. The studies concern ageing faces; use in young men is discussed in forums.

lead: A cheek lift, also called a midface lift, is a cosmetic surgical procedure that repositions sagging soft tissue of the cheek, including the malar fat pad, to a higher position on the face. It is performed under the broader heading of facial rejuvenation and is often combined with eyelid surgery or a full facelift [1][2].

Surgical descriptions in the literature include approaches through the lower eyelid, through the mouth and hairline, and by endoscope, with some techniques working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering the facial bones [3][4][5]. Non-surgical alternatives that are marketed for lifting the cheeks, such as threads, fillers and energy-based devices, are discussed separately from surgical cheek lifts [6][7].

In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mainly by younger men who report a hollow or aged look in the midface and ask how much a cheek lift would improve their appearance. Published evidence on the procedure is largely surgeon-authored technique descriptions rather than controlled trials.
infobox: Cheek flattening, nasolabial fold laxity, malar fat pad descent

paras: General references describe the midface lift as aimed at people whose main concern is flattening of the cheeks and deepening of the fold between nose and mouth, without marked jowling or neck laxity. Small incisions at the hairline and inside the mouth are used so that the fat pads over the cheekbones can be moved upward, which typically leaves few visible scars [1].

Surgeons have published several named variations. A 1999 report described a simplified subperiosteal cheek lift performed through the lower eyelid, developed as a modification of earlier endoscopic and eyelid-approach methods because the earlier eyelid approach required a lateral canthoplasty that added technical difficulty and risk of complications [2]. A 1998 paper described a subperiosteal approach to the midface termed the tridimensional functional cheek lift [4]. A 2017 report in Archives of Plastic Surgery described a technique titled facial rejuvenation enhancing cheek lift [5].

Cheek volume can also be addressed without repositioning tissue. A 2005 review of facial sculpting discussed dermal and subdermal fillers used to support the brow, the tear-trough area and the malar region, as part of an expansion of fillers into roles formerly handled by surgery [6]. Thread lifts, which use suture threads to suspend tissue, are described as a minimally invasive option, though a general reference notes concern over variable training of practitioners [7][8].
In Asian patients with prominent cheekbones, a 2016 report described combining reduction malarplasty with a facelift to counter cheek descent that can follow bone reduction in older patients [9].

General facelift references list haematoma, nerve injury, scarring, hair loss at incisions and, in smokers, skin necrosis among the complications of facial lifting surgery [1]. Midface-specific publications in the literature include reports on lower-eyelid malposition and retraction as a complication of eyelid and cheek surgery, treated with revision procedures [10][11]. A 2005 study also examined the effect of rhytidectomy on the nasal valve [12].

Published surgical literature on cheek lifts consists mostly of technique descriptions and case series by the surgeons who developed the methods [2][4][5]. The sources available here do not report randomised comparisons of surgical cheek lifts.

Registered trials exist for non-surgical lifting products and devices in the midface. These include a completed 144-participant trial of hyaluronic-acid-coated and uncoated threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction [13], a completed 103-participant study of an ultrasound system for lifting and tightening cheek tissue [14], a 45-participant trial of a laser-type device for lax skin [15] and a 45-participant study combining threads with microfocused ultrasound [16]. Their results are not summarised in the registry records cited here.

A 2011 study quantified errors that arise when standardised facial photography is not followed, noting that photographs are used for documentation of before-and-after results in plastic surgery and that subtle changes are easy to misjudge in non-standard images [17].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, cheek lifts come up as a hardmaxx option for men who feel their cheeks look flat or aged; discussion is small and mostly consists of users asking how much it would change their rating [18].

claims.claim: A cheek lift would make a large difference to how old and attractive a young man looks.
Tanning, cardio and lower body fat can reduce the aged look of the malar area without surgery.
Facial exercises quickly reduce the appearance of malar fat pads.

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer is reportedly the first to perform a facelift, in general reference accounts of the procedure's history [1].
A subperiosteal midface approach called the tridimensional functional cheek lift is published [4].
A simplified transblepharoplasty subperiosteal cheek lift is described [2].
A cheek-lift technique is described in Archives of Plastic Surgery [5].
